domain: Technology Governance / Constitutional Law / Platform Economics
topic_summary: Analysis of content moderation obligations imposed on private social media platforms, examining the structural tension between platforms as private property exercising editorial discretion versus platforms as essential public infrastructure subject to common carrier or state action obligations. The topic encompasses First Amendment constraints, Section 230 immunity, state-level moderation laws, and the collision between platform business models and democratic speech norms.

key_entities: Social media platforms (Meta, X/Twitter, YouTube — private corporations with editorial control)
U.S. Federal Government (First Amendment enforcer; Section 230 grantor)
State governments (Texas, Florida — attempting moderation regulation)
Content moderators (human and algorithmic enforcement agents)
key_tensions: Platform editorial discretion vs state-imposed neutrality mandates (private property vs common carrier framing)
Section 230 immunity vs publisher liability (legal shield enabling moderation vs accountability gap)
Democratic speech norms vs advertiser-driven content policy (public forum expectations vs private business model)
key_mechanisms: Section 230(c)(2) 'Good Samaritan' provision (federal immunity for moderation decisions)
Algorithmic content ranking and suppression (automated enforcement at scale)
Advertiser boycott pressure (economic mechanism shaping moderation policy)
key_absences: International jurisdiction collision (EU Digital Services Act vs U.S. First Amendment framework)
Platform market concentration effects (whether oligopoly status changes obligation analysis)

axes.human_readable: Private Property vs Public Forum (Constitutional Status of Platforms)
axes.structural_delta: Whether platforms are private editorial entities protected by First Amendment or quasi-public forums subject to neutrality obligations
axes.primary_observable: Supreme Court precedent on state action doctrine applied to platforms; constitutional status in Moody v NetChoice and similar cases
axes.selection_reason: Highest centrality; foundational constitutional framing that structures all downstream obligations

axes.structural_delta: Extent to which federal law immunizes platforms from liability for user content and moderation decisions
axes.primary_observable: Circuit court interpretations of Section 230(c)(1) and (c)(2); legislative proposals to narrow immunity
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable (statutory interpretation vs constitutional status); coordination mechanism structuring platform behavior

axes.structural_delta: Whether state laws mandating content neutrality or disclosure survive First Amendment and preemption challenges
axes.primary_observable: Judicial outcomes in NetChoice v Paxton (Texas) and NetChoice v Moody (Florida); circuit splits on compelled speech doctrine
axes.selection_reason: Different structural delta from Section 230 (state vs federal authority); independent epsilon measuring state regulatory power

axes.human_readable: Advertiser-Driven Moderation (Economic Constraint on Speech Policy)
axes.structural_delta: Platform moderation policy shaped by advertiser brand safety demands rather than legal obligation or democratic norms
axes.primary_observable: Correlation between advertiser boycotts and policy changes; brand safety certification requirements
axes.selection_reason: Independent observable (economic pressure vs legal mandate); distinct beneficiary structure; captures non-legal extraction mechanism

axes.human_readable: Moderation Liability Exposure (Over-Removal vs Under-Removal Risk)
axes.structural_delta: Platform liability risk from both excessive moderation (viewpoint discrimination claims) and insufficient moderation (harm facilitation claims)
axes.primary_observable: Litigation rates for wrongful removal vs failure-to-remove; insurance costs; settlement patterns
axes.selection_reason: Downstream synthesis node; captures the operational double-bind created by upstream legal and economic constraints

axes.primary_observable: Regulatory proposals requiring algorithmic transparency; judicial treatment of ranking as speech vs conduct

omegas.description: Does EU Digital Services Act mandatory moderation create de facto global standard that overrides U.S. First Amendment framework? If so, the constitutional status axis becomes subordinate to extraterritorial regulation.

If Section 230 is repealed or substantially narrowed, does the liability exposure axis collapse into a single high-epsilon snare, or does it bifurcate into publisher liability (high epsilon) vs distributor liability (low epsilon)?

Is the private property vs public forum axis stable, or does Supreme Court state action doctrine evolution (e.g., Halleck, Manhattan Community Access) reclassify platforms as state actors subject to First Amendment neutrality obligations?

Is advertiser-driven moderation a distributed snare (many independent actors) or a coordinated cartel (GARM, brand safety consortia)? If coordinated, epsilon increases and antitrust implications emerge.
